text.p: European mediation in the Middle East made a breakthrough in Malta on Wednesday when the Europeans arranged a meeting between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo took Levy up to see Arafat at a Valletta hotel after two days of wrangling over Palestinian conditions for such a meeting.
Arafat spokesman Marwan Kanafani described it as a courtesy call on Arafat but added that the Israeli had 20 minutes separately with Palestinian Planning Minister Nabil Shaath.

"There was a cordial and very warm exchange of ideas and recommitments to the peace process. No substance was discussed except that both leaders agreed that there should be a real attempt to go back to the peace process," he added.

"We consider this as a positive step, as a good goodwill step and hopefully we will take it from there and with the help of the European Union go ahead and start to put the peace process back on the right track," he said.
Levy, speaking in Hebrew through an interpreter, said progress had been made but differences remained. Back in Israel, he would "define the parameters for returning to negotiations", he added.
Shaath, asked if a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would now be possible, said: "Not at this stage. This is just the beginning."
The meetings were at the highest level since Netanyahu decided last month to go ahead with a Jewish settlement in disputed Arab East Jerusalem.
Since then Palestinians have clashed daily with Israeli troops in the West Bank and the Palestinians have called off their security cooperation with the Israeli authorities.
The direct talks in Malta were a surprise twist to roller- coaster Middle East diplomacy at a conference of foreign ministers from 27 European and Mediterranean ministers.

They also gave an unexpected shot in the arm to Europe's attempts to find a role in the Middle East peace process, alongside or in friendly competition with the United States, the traditional go-between.
U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross arrives back in the region on Wednesday on a mission to put Israeli-Palestinian talks back on track after the setbacks of the last month.
Most delegates had written off the chances of the Europeans arranging direct talks between Israel and the Palestinians.
It was not immediately clear what had persuaded the Palestinians to agree to the meeting. Earlier they had said it would be pointless as Levy had nothing new to offer.
The atmosphere at the conference earlier on Wednesday had been uniformly gloomy as disagreements on Middle East peace weighed heavily on the rest of the agenda.
The Dutch presidency of the European Union had tried to set up direct talks between Israel and the Palestinians on Tuesday but the attempt appeared to collapse.

Arafat spokesman Marwan Kanafani said on Tuesday night that the chances of a meeting hardly existed. Even plans for a goodwill meeting between Levy and a Palestinian such as Planning Minister Nabil Shaath had unravelled, he said.
"They would have nothing to talk about," one Palestinian delegate said of the impasse.

"From what we hear Mr Levy has nothing new to offer. There is no change in Israeli policy on Jerusalem or settlements in general. I don't know of any real progress that has been achieved here," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Wednesday morning, shortly before the meeting took place.
"I don't think the (Middle East) peace process will happen here," added French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

In parallel with the arguments over the terms for a meeting, Israel and the Arab states took the conference to the wire on how the ministers should handle the Middle East peace section of the final statement.

The Europeans are anxious to keep the Arab-Israeli conflict out of the limelight and would be happy with a text which repeats what they said in Barcelona in 1995 at the launching of this European-Mediterranean dialogue.
That text specifies that a settlement should be based on the principle of land for peace -- a principle which Netanyahu's rightwing government has questioned.
Delegates said both Israel and the Arabs had their own ideas about what the conference should say and that senior officials were trying to find a compromise.
The Arabs want a reference to Israel's settlement policies, seen in the Arab world as a violation of international law and of agreements reached earlier in peace talks.

Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara told the conference earlier on Wednesday that the 18-month-old partnership between Europe and Mediterranean countries could be threatened by conflict in the Middle East.

"A firm stand by the European Union supported by practical measures taken vis-a-vis the Israeli policies and practices would certainly help salvage the peace process and put it back on track," he said.
